title: Leap Year Checker
story: Your calendar app keeps getting February wrong — sometimes 28 days, sometimes 29. You decide to solve this once and for all by coding the leap year rule: a year is a leap year if it's divisible by 4, UNLESS it's also divisible by 100, UNLESS it's also divisible by 400.
why: The leap year rule is a classic Boolean logic puzzle that combines AND, OR, and NOT into one compact function — the kind of logic used everywhere from calendars to access control.
analogy: The leap year rule is like a VIP club entrance. Rule 1: If you're on the 400 list (divisible by 400), you're in. Rule 2: If you're on the banned-100 list (divisible by 100), you're out — even if you were on the 4 list. Rule 3: If you're on the 4 list, you're in. Otherwise, denied. The order of checking the lists at the door is critical — check the VIP 400 list first!
try_it: Extend is_leap_year to print WHY each year is or isn't a leap year. For example: '2000 is a leap year because it is divisible by 400.' Add years 2100, 2400, and your birth year to the test set.
tips: Order is crucial: 400 check before 100 check before 4 check
Each `if` returns immediately — only one branch can execute per call
Use `%` (modulo) to check divisibility: `year % 4 == 0` means divisible by 4
The final `return false` catches all non-special years (common years)
common_mistakes: Checking % 100 before % 400 — the year 2000 would be wrong
Writing `year / 4` instead of `year % 4` — division gives quotient, not remainder
Combining conditions with confusing AND/OR instead of cascading if statements
Forgetting the final `return false` for non-leap years
